headlines.title: New numbers show odds spike for major Bay Area earthquake in next 30 years
headlines.description: The risk of a large earthquake in the Bay Area has just been recalculated and the odds have gone up. New federal numbers put the odds of a magnitude 6.7 quake or stronger in the Bay Area during the next 30 years at 74.1% — up from 72% from a previous study. “It’s reinforcing what we already know,” United States Geological Survey geophysicist Kevin Milner said. “That we have to be prepared for a major earthquake. It is going to happen in most of our lifetimes.” The updated numbers come from the USGS, which did its first estimate in 2014. Milner co-authored the first study and conducted the new one. He said the more time that passes without a major quake, the higher the probability of having one. Stanford University Aug 25 East Bay Aug 13 The Hayward-Rodgers Creek Fault System, which stretches from San Jose to the San Pablo Bay, still has the highest probability of producing a magnitude 6.7 or stronger earthquake. But the biggest increase is on the San Andreas Fault up 3.6% to 25.5%. That fault stretches from Southern California through the Bay Area and north toward Eureka. It also produced the devastating 1906 earthquake, as well as the Loma Prieta quake in 1989. As the earthquake risk rises, so does the potential for damage — especially to critical infastructure. Victor Zayas, president of Earthquake Protection Systems, said while building standards have made major advances, more protections are needed. “If we build any buildings, especially any new hospitals, we should be building them to not be damaged by earthquakes, not just not collapse,” Zayas said. USGS is working on developing new models to better understand earthquakes and their risks.

headlines.title: San Jose's Regional Medical Center adds 20 ER beds amid growing demand
headlines.description: Regional Medical Center in San Jose is increasing its emergency room capacity by nearly 60% in an effort to reduce patient wait times. A new section of the emergency department opened Wednesday afternoon, adding 20 beds as part of a $17 million expansion project. Some of the new beds are in private rooms. The expansion brings the emergency department’s total capacity to 53 beds. The new beds are expected to fill up quickly. Regional Medical Center accounts for 30% of emergency room visits among hospitals operated by Santa Clara County. “These additional beds mean we can move patients in to get medications and treatments more quickly, decreasing their wait times and decreasing the wait for relief from their symptoms,” said Dr. Yvonne Karanas, physician executive at Regional Medical Center. County leaders said the additional capacity is needed as demand for emergency services at county hospitals continues to grow. Emergency department demand has increased 10% over the past two years and is expected to rise further. Santa Clara County Executive James Williams said cuts in federal health care funding could leave more people without access to routine exams, potentially leaving some with no option other than seeking care in emergency departments. While many nurses welcome the additional beds, the president of the Registered Nurses Professional Association said expanding capacity alone is not enough. “The county needs to step up and have more nurses so we will be able to accommodate the expansion,” association President Allan Kamara said. Regional Medical Center’s emergency department recently treated nearly 300 patients in a single day. Officials hope the expansion will help future patients receive treatment more quickly.

headlines.title: 49ers set to embark on NFL's longest road trip for season opener in Australia
headlines.description: The San Francisco 49ers got instructions for how to prepare for the longest road trip in NFL history as they get set to depart the Bay Area for Melbourne, Australia, late Wednesday night for the season opener against the Los Angeles Rams next week. They were given advice on how to eat and hydrate, what to do after arriving and the best options of when to sleep on the approximately 8,000-mile flight that will take about 16 hours and cross the international dateline that will make a Wednesday departure turn into a Friday arrival. Niners defensive lineman and avid world traveler Keion White has a simple approach. “I don’t know if you can OD on melatonin, but I’m going to try,” he said. “Take five melatonins, go to sleep on the plane. As soon as I wake up, I’m taking five more. Just keep rolling like that.” While some members of the 49ers organization, including coach Kyle Shanahan, have been lamenting the season-opening trip, White is embracing it after already playing games in Germany and London earlier in his career. He plans to watch TikTok before he arrives to get ideas of what to do and then get on public transportation and explore after team meetings on the first day to help make sure he stays up all day and gets onto a normal sleep schedule as quickly as possible. “I’m an experience guy,” he said. “If I’m up, walking around, just going to go do stuff, I’ll be up. Just go explore. We will have meetings and everything like that, but once I do that, I’m out exploring Melbourne and getting around town.” Both the 49ers and Rams studied the process intently in the offseason, even sending advance staffers to Australia to report back on how long it took to adjust to the time change. But they came up with far different answers leading up to the game on Sept. 11. The Niners will leave Wednesday night in California, arrive in Melbourne on Friday morning and then take time to adjust to the new time zone. They will hold a light practice on Saturday, take Sunday off and then have a normal stretch of three practices on Monday through Wednesday before playing the opener on Friday morning. They will leave right after the game and are expected to land back in the Bay Area on Friday afternoon. They then will be able to take the weekend off before preparing for the Week 2 game against Miami on Sept. 20. “It’s a big adjustment on the body,” Shanahan said. “So, the recommendation for everybody has been to tell us when to go, and it’s made a lot of sense. I know how our players feel also. I was a little bit on the fence. Science wasn’t and what I was reported on and our players weren’t at all. So that helped me get off the fence.” The Rams consulted with their own scientists and came up with the opposite approach. They will do most of their practice at home and aren’t expected to arrive in Australia until about 24 hours before the game, hoping the short stay leads to no jet lag. The better option might not be known until after the game. The approach by the Niners has made the past few days a whirlwind. The players got the weekend off after playing the final exhibition game on Thursday night in Las Vegas and resumed practice on Monday — the day after the roster was reduced to 53 players. The front office had to make those cuts, put together a practice squad and figure out which players would be healthy for Week 1 to make sure they had the correct roster in place before departing. “There’s a lot behind the scenes,” general manager John Lynch said. “Our logistics folks, our folks that work in the cafe, have just gone to tremendous lengths, our health and performance team, to make sure that we’re giving our players the best opportunity to feel right when they play down there in Australia. Everything from getting visas, which much more complicated than I ever knew, and they’ve been outstanding. … Hats off to those guys for pulling off a monumental task, and it’s not done yet.” Lynch said he had to make sure all the practice squad players he wanted to sign had passports with one needing his parents to send it overnight. It was an even bigger scramble for offensive lineman Jarrett Patterson, who was acquired in a trade from Houston on Sunday. “They were like, hey, do you have a passport? We’re leaving for Australia in three days,” he said. “I was like, ‘Whoa!’ It’s obviously a quick turnaround getting here a couple hours after I found out and now getting ready for Australia.” But in all, the players are welcoming the challenge and opportunity. Cornerback Deommodore Lenoir said he’d travel 30 hours if needed to play in an NFL game and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling has a must-see item on his to-do list before making his debut. “I kind of want to see a kangaroo, just because,” he said. “To see how big they are.” ___ See AP’s full NFL coverage here

headlines.title: 2 men killed in wrong-way crash in Santa Clara identified
headlines.description: Two men who died in a fiery, wrong-way crash in Santa Clara last week have been identified, the Santa Clara County Medical Examiner’s Office announced Wednesday. On Aug. 26, police responded to Montague Expressway at the Lafayette Street overpass where they found a GMC SUV on its side and engulfed in flames, and a damaged silver Honda pickup truck. Investigators believe that the SUV driver was driving in the wrong direction on northbound Montague Expressway and collided with the Honda. The people killed in the crash were 58-year-old Stephen Hinkson of San Carlos and 39-year-old Keith Demarest, whose city of residence was not released. Information on who drove which vehicle was not immediately available.

headlines.title: San Francisco welcomes new Alioto's Plaza at Fisherman's Wharf
headlines.description: San Francisco gave a warm welcome to the new Alioto’s Plaza at Fisherman’s Wharf Wednesday, which offers a new public space for people who live, work and visit the area. “For nearly 100 years, this site was the home to Alioto’s, a restaurant that helped define the wharf. When it closed in March of 2020, the empty building became a visible reminder of what this neighborhood endured during the pandemic,” Mayor Daniel Lurie said. The plaza expands the view and access to the inner harbor with its rich history. Lurie says the plaza is giving people a reason to return. The plaza it’s another connection to the water at Fisherman’s Wharf that welcomes tourists, neighbors and workers. The city says more than 15 restaurants and businesses have opened since 2025, and soon a new taproom will open its doors. “We’ve been looking at Fisherman’s Wharf for a long time, being from the city, I have fond memories and I thought it was some sort of ripe for a rejuvenation and wanted to be part of it,” CEO of Woods Beer and Wine Company Jim Woods said. Members of the business community think it will be an important feature during Fleet Week and Labor Day. The Port is also looking at the future. “The Port sees this plaza as step one in plans to continue to invest in seismic resilience and public space regeneration here at wharf this is a plaza a place that respects the wharf’s history while creating new space for what comes next,” Executive Director Port of San Francisco Michael Martin said.

headlines.title: 12th annual San Francisco Chinatown's Night Out to be hosted at a different venue
headlines.description: The 12th annual San Francisco Chinatown’s Night Out will be celebrated on Sept. 9 at a new venue. The event is intended to introduce the community to the cops and their commanders assigned to the area. “Public safety works best when officers build strong relationships with the people they serve. When beat officers know the store owners on their block. When an officer stops to help a senior, and when public safety workers know the neighborhood, and know the people who they’re there to protect,” Mayor Daniel Lurie said. With Portsmouth Square still under construction, Willie “Woo Woo” Wong Playground Park will be the site of the annual Chinatown Night Out. Organizers say about 1,000 people usually show up, each gets a meal and a grab bag full of goodies. Willie “Woo Woo” Wong has become one of the default parks in the neighborhood for seniors and others as Portsmouth Square goes through a major renovation. For SFPD this year, there’s also a feeling of accomplishment because crime rates continue to fall across the city. “We are down 20% across the board in all crime categories. And that’s already on top of historic lows from last year as well, so, I’m really happy of that result,” San Francisco Police Chief Derrick Lew said. In 2025, the city experienced a 30% drop in crime. In 2026, some categories are also at historic lows, including car break ins, which are the lowest in 23 years. Chinatown Night Out is also an opportunity for public safety departments to connect with community members. Fire Chief Dean Crispen says they are working with seniors in the neighborhood. “To create a placard that folks can put on their refrigerator, so that when EMT’s and paramedics respond, there’s communication about the medical issues and the medications the folks are taking,” Crispen said. The event is free and everyone is invited to join.

headlines.title: This dime sold for $1.2 million. The story behind its extraordinary value
headlines.description: With its darkened silver surface and coppery-gold hues, the more than 130-year-old dime may not look especially remarkable at first glance. But the 1894-S Barber dime is considered one of the rarest coins in American numismatics. On Sept. 1, one example sold for $1,250,500 at auction, more than 260 times the amount a teenage collector paid for it nearly seven decades ago. That collector was Q. David Bowers, who purchased the coin for $4,750 at age 19 in 1957. The headline-grabbing purchase helped launch what would become a prominent career in the rare-coin world, but the story behind the dime stretches back much further. The coin’s value comes largely from its rarity. Minted in San Francisco in 1894, the dime was produced during a period of economic hardship following the Panic of 1893, when demand for newly minted currency had declined sharply. As a result, the San Francisco Mint struck just 24 of the coins in June 1894. Today, only nine examples are confirmed to exist, though experts believe others may have survived. Because so few are known, and many remain in private collections for years or even decades, opportunities to buy one are exceptionally rare. scams 11 hours ago Food & Drink Apr 25 “The mere mention of this coin is enough to attract the attention of even casual collectors,” auction house Stack’s Bowers said, describing the 1894-S as one of the classic rarities in coin collecting. Bowers recognized the coin’s significance when it came up for auction in 1957 with an estimated value of $5,000. He ultimately purchased it for $4,750, a sum that drew national attention at the time. “In 1957, I paid the record price of $4,750 for a beautiful uncirculated 1894-S dime,” Bowers wrote in a 2015 column for Coin World. He later sold the coin for $6,000, though its value continued to rise dramatically over the following decades. Before this year’s sale, only five 1894-S Barber dimes had appeared at auction since 2005, according to Stack’s Bowers. Those coins sold for between $1.3 million and $2.16 million. The example once owned by Bowers had not appeared at auction in 36 years. It previously sold for $77,000 in 1987 and $93,500 in 1990. This year, it returned to the auction block with an estimated value of $1.5 million. On Sept. 1, the coin sold for $1,250,500, adding another chapter to the story of one of the rarest dimes ever produced. This story was originally reported in Spanish for Telemundo.

headlines.title: What is Kalshi and why is it so controversial?
headlines.description: Kalshi, one of the fastest growing companies in the world (but also one of the most controversial) calls itself a prediction market, even when many consider it a gambling site. Kalshi was banned in Nevada, a move that the company says was wrong. Kalshi is where millions of people go to place what it calls “trades,” what some call “bets” on events. The company makes money by charging a transaction fee on every trade. Kalshi is currently being sued by four states, but it’s also wildly successful, as it was being valued by investors at $22 billion as of Wednesday. Scott Budman explains what Kalshi is all about in the video above.

headlines.title: Man rescued from inside garbage truck in San Francisco
headlines.description: A man was rescued from inside a garbage truck early Wednesday morning in San Francisco, according to the fire department. Firefighters were dispatched around 4:11 a.m. to the 100 block of Mason Street following a report of a person trapped inside a Recology garbage truck. According to SFFD, the truck’s driver had been flagged down and told that someone could be heard yelling from inside the garbage area of the truck. About 25 firefighters responded to the scene, and the rescue operation took roughly two hours, according to fire officials. The man was eventually rescued and was conscious, breathing and talking before being taken to a hospital, according to a San Francisco Fire Department spokesperson. The extent of his injuries was not immediately known. A firefighter also suffered a laceration to the hand during the rescue and was taken to a hospital for stitches, fire officials added. A fire official said he is believed to have entered a dumpster looking for food before he got trapped in the garbage truck. Bay City News contributed to this report
headlines.source: Joel Soria and Ginger Conejero Saab

headlines.title: AI boom heats up Bay Area housing market as wealthy buyers drive demand for high-end homes across U.S.
headlines.description: Here’s another place the AI frenzy is making itself felt: the market for luxury homes. High-income earners, many of them employees at AI companies, are snapping up multimillion-dollar houses in the San Francisco Bay Area, undaunted by the higher mortgage rates and rising home prices that have prevented many would-be buyers from affording a home. The Bay Area buying spree is the clearest manifestation of a nationwide trend of sales of upper-end properties largely holding up better than sales of less expensive homes. Metro areas such as San Diego, Miami, Detroit, Nashville and Tampa, Florida, are also seeing upper-market homes sell at a faster pace. The hotter market for luxury properties comes at a time when the broader housing market remains stuck in a yearslong rut. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, moored at a 30-year low. Most recently, they slowed again in July. Sales of newly built homes, which make up a far smaller part of the housing market, are also down this year. Underpinning the luxury market are affluent home shoppers who can afford to shrug off rising mortgage rates and often pay all cash for a home or come up with a large down payment by raising funds through sales of stocks or other investments. Stock market gains powered by the artificial intelligence boom have helped boost investors’ portfolios. The benchmark S&P 500 is up solidly this year and remains near its most recent all-time high. “These people have lots of money and they’re just not going to be very sensitive to things like mortgage rates or home prices,” said Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin. “They want the home they want and they have the money to buy it.” The trend is the housing market version of the “K-shaped” economy, where wealthier households pull ahead of middle- and lower-income ones. In this case, many would-be homebuyers remain on the sideline while affluent buyers drive sales of luxury homes. Sales of pricier homes are holding up better Nationally, sales of luxury homes, defined as properties in the top 5% of a metro area by price, rose 2% in the first half of this year, compared to the same period in 2025, according to data from Redfin. Sales of middle-of-the-market homes, or properties closest to an area’s median price, rose 1.9% in the same period. The dichotomy in the market can better be seen in price appreciation. The median sales price of a luxury home nationally between January and June was roughly $1.37 million, a 4.3% increase from a year earlier. For homes in the middle of the market, the median sales price rose 1.4% to $377,245. In the San Francisco metro area, sales of luxury homes soared 39.3% in the first half of this year compared to a year earlier, while middle-market home sales surged 15.1%. And across the bay in Oakland, sales of upper-market homes jumped 13.3%, while sales of middle-market properties rose 3.9%. Several other metro areas not plugged into the AI boom are also seeing sales and price growth for luxury homes. Among the most notable examples: in the Tampa metro area, luxury home sales surged 35.5% in the January-June period, while sales of middle-market homes fell 5.1%. In Nashville, sales of upper-market homes jumped 10.8%, while sales of middle-market properties rose only 1.7%. And in Detroit, sales of higher-end properties vaulted 8.7% compared to a 6% decline in sales of middle-market homes. All told, sales of luxury homes so far this year are outpacing or have declined less than those of middle-market homes in 44% of the nation’s 50 largest metro areas. Urgency to buy a home before potential AI IPOs In the Bay Area, tech companies bent on winning the race to develop artificial intelligence into a profitable business have juiced compensation to recruit talented executives and software engineers, widening the pool of high-income earners. Many of these employees have been buying homes, often outdoing rival buyers by offering well above the asking price, real estate agents say. The Bay Area housing market could get even hotter should two of the biggest names in AI follow through on their intent to become publicly traded companies. OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, and Anthropic, home to Claude, filed preliminary paperwork in June for initial public offerings. Neither has yet decided on the timing. An analysis by Redfin that looked at how much employees at both companies stand to gain potentially from the companies going public estimated that the combined IPO earnings would be enough to buy nearly one-third of all homes in San Francisco. Just the possibility of these two blockbuster IPOs is building pressure on some home shoppers in the Bay Area to buy sooner, rather than later. They worry they’ll face a flood of newly minted millionaires ready to pounce, further ratcheting up competition in the San Francisco housing market. Julio Bermudez, an AI data infrastructure company executive in the Bay Area, had been looking to buy his first home for about a year, but his search took on new urgency. “So, you start taking a look at that and you take a look at your own position — both from just a diversification standpoint, as well as the fact that we’re trying to set roots here, kids are in school, all that good stuff,” said Bermudez, 41. ”And it’s like we don’t want to be priced out, so we need to buy now.” Recently, Bermudez entered into a contract to buy a five-bedroom, four-bath house in Orinda, about 17 miles northeast of San Francisco. The seller was asking $3.5 million, but agreed to sell for $3.3 million. “I felt like this was sort of an interesting time and location to try to strike before it really does get crazy,” he said.

headlines.title: SF high school's varsity baseball coaching staff removed after racial incident
headlines.description: A San Francisco high school has lost its entire varsity baseball coaching staff and must forfeit some games following a racial incident. The San Francisco Unified School District did not elaborate on what happened, but the San Francisco Chronicle reported it involved alleged race-based taunting by Lowell High School varsity players during a game in May against Lincoln High School. Following an investigation by the school district, the varsity coaching staff at Lowell has been removed and the school will forfeit regular season games against three schools, including Lincoln. In a statement, the district said, “…there is no place for racism, discrimination, or racialized harm in the Lowell community or anywhere in SFUSD.” Parents said it’s difficult to know if the district made the right call because it didn’t release enough details about the incident.

headlines.title: Bay Area rail agencies highlight risks near tracks
headlines.description: More people die in rail-related incidents in California than in any other state, and officials say most of those deaths are preventable. Bay Area rail agencies gathered Wednesday at Diridon Station in San Jose to raise awareness about railroad safety and dangerous behavior around crossings. Representatives from Union Pacific, VTA, Caltrain, Amtrak, Capitol Corridor and other agencies displayed safety equipment and handed out educational materials as part of the safety effort. NBC Bay Area got a firsthand look at some of those dangers during a ride aboard a Union Pacific locomotive. Before boarding the locomotive, NBC Bay Area saw one driver stopped on the tracks and others stopped too close to the rails. From inside the conductor’s cab, a person was seen jogging around lowered crossing gates while warning alarms were sounding. Unhoused people were also seen camping and walking within feet of the tracks. Other drivers were seen making unsafe U-turns rather than waiting for the crossing gates to rise. Between 2020 and 2024, 593 people died in rail-related incidents in California, according to the latest available statistics. California also accounts for 24% of trespassing deaths, the highest percentage in the nation. According to the Federal Railroad Administration, 94% of deaths are caused by risky driver behavior.
